supporting_references.why_relevant: This planning document supports the benchmark’s emphasis on city-led network planning, route expansion, and safety-oriented cycling investment rather than generic recreation or commuting analysis.

cases.title: Traffic burden near vulnerable communities

supporting_references.why_relevant: Directly supports the unequal-burden framing: traffic is a major PM2.5 source in NYC, impacts are more acute in less wealthy neighborhoods, and traffic-related PM2.5 is reported as higher in high-poverty neighborhoods.

supporting_references.title: New York City’s Environmental Justice for All Report Scope of Work
supporting_references.why_relevant: Provides city policy grounding for environmental-justice screening and prioritization across neighborhoods.

cases.title: Air pollution and neighborhood disadvantage
cases.query: A public-health or environmental-justice analyst wants to identify NYC neighborhoods where higher ambient air pollution overlaps with socioeconomic disadvantage. Using the available data catalog, select the air-pollution, poverty, and unemployment datasets needed for a credible screening analysis, choose the most defensible common geography or harmonization step, and explain what the resulting screen can and cannot support for health-equity reporting.
cases.why_relevant: This is a strong benchmark for dataset selection under geography mismatch, not just for naming an air-quality file.
cases.source_hint: NYC Health: The public health impacts of PM2.5 from traffic air pollution; Air quality data for NYC

supporting_references.title: NYC Community Air Survey (NYCCAS)
supporting_references.type: official NYC Health report / data feature
supporting_references.what_it_supports: NYCCAS is NYC’s long-running neighborhood air-monitoring program. The report explicitly says it presents **maps of neighborhood air pollution levels by year** and identifies local sources driving differences across neighborhoods. It also notes that PM2.5, NO2, NO, and black carbon are highest in areas with greater traffic density, building density, warehouses, and commercial cooking.
supporting_references.why_it_matters_for_this_benchmark: This directly grounds a neighborhood-level burden-screening task rather than a citywide summary.

supporting_references.title: NYC Health: *The public health impacts of PM2.5 from traffic air pollution*
supporting_references.what_it_supports: The page states that traffic-related PM2.5 impacts are not evenly distributed across the city and that **PM2.5 levels from all traffic sources are about 50% higher in high-poverty neighborhoods than in low-poverty neighborhoods**.
supporting_references.why_it_matters_for_this_benchmark: This is the clearest official justification for combining an air-pollution burden layer with poverty-related neighborhood disadvantage in an environmental-justice framing.

supporting_references.title: NYC Community Air Survey landing page
supporting_references.what_it_supports: The page explains that NYCCAS was created to evaluate how air quality differs across NYC neighborhoods and notes the addition of **environmental justice sites** to better understand emissions in low-income neighborhoods.
supporting_references.why_it_matters_for_this_benchmark: It reinforces that NYCCAS is intended for neighborhood-scale inequality analysis, not just for generic pollution mapping.

supporting_references.title: Air quality data for NYC
supporting_references.what_it_supports: The page states that health impacts from fine particulate matter, black carbon, and sulfur dioxide are higher in high-poverty neighborhoods.
supporting_references.why_it_matters_for_this_benchmark: It is the clearest direct NYC statement that air-pollution burden and neighborhood disadvantage overlap in practice.

cases.notes: A strong benchmark answer should not assume that NTAs are the right join target.
